title: Bullying and harassment at work
summary: What bullying looks like, where it happens, how harassment linked to a protected characteristic differs, and what to do if you think it is happening to you.

sections.title: What bullying is
sections.body:
Bullying has no formal legal definition. In general, it is unwelcome conduct from a person or a group that is hurtful, or that misuses power to demean or harm someone.
It can be a repeated pattern of behaviour, or a single event that is serious enough to hurt someone.
key_points: Bullying has no formal legal definition
It is unwelcome conduct that hurts or misuses power
It can be a pattern or a single serious event

sections.title: Examples of bullying
sections.body:
Examples include relentless criticism of someone's work, spreading nasty gossip, belittling someone in meetings, piling extra work on someone unfairly, and leaving someone out of team events.
Posting demeaning content about a colleague online is also bullying.
key_points: Spreading gossip and belittling people in meetings
Unfairly piling on work, or leaving someone out

sections.title: Where and how it happens
sections.body:
Bullying can happen in person, online, or through messages and calls. It can happen at work or in other work-related settings, such as a work trip.
The person doing it may not realise that their behaviour is bullying, and may not mean to cause harm. That does not make it acceptable.
key_points: It can happen in person, online, by message or by call
It can happen in any work-related setting
Intent does not decide whether it is bullying

sections.title: Bullying can go up as well as down
sections.body:
Bullying is not only a manager picking on staff. It can also be aimed upward at a senior person, through disrespect, refusing reasonable tasks or undermining their authority.
All of it matters, and each case should be looked at on its facts.
key_points: Bullying can be aimed at a manager as well as by one
Each case should be looked at on its facts

sections.title: Harassment linked to a protected characteristic
sections.body:
Harassment is different from general bullying in one respect. Under the Equality Act 2010, harassment is unwanted conduct that is related to a protected characteristic, such as race, sex or disability.
Harassment does not need to be intended to count. What matters is the effect it has on the person.
key_points: Harassment is unwanted conduct linked to a protected characteristic
It can count even when it was not intended

sections.title: If you think you are being bullied
sections.body:
Write down what happened, when, and who was there, while it is fresh. Raise it with your manager or with HR, following your organisation's policy.
If you are not sure what to do, the Acas helpline gives free advice on bullying and harassment at work.
key_points: Keep a written record while the details are fresh
Raise it with your manager or HR
Acas can advise on bullying and harassment

questions.prompt: Does bullying have a formal legal definition?
options: Yes, a fixed definition in one statute
No, it has no formal legal definition
questions.explanation: Bullying has no formal legal definition. In general it means unwelcome conduct that hurts or misuses power.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of bullying?
options: Spreading nasty gossip about a colleague
Asking for a report by Friday
questions.explanation: Spreading nasty gossip is an example of bullying. Feedback and reasonable requests are part of normal work.

options: Yes, including through messages and calls
Only on social media outside work
questions.explanation: Bullying can happen in person, online, or through messages and calls, at work or in other work-related settings.

questions.prompt: Can a single incident be bullying?
options: It can be, as well as a repeated pattern
Only if it is written down
questions.explanation: Bullying can be a repeated pattern or a single serious event.

questions.prompt: For harassment linked to a protected characteristic, must the person doing it intend the effect?
options: No, the conduct can count whether or not it was intended
Only if they are a manager
questions.explanation: Harassment under the Equality Act does not need to be intended. What matters is the effect of the conduct.
